actionable.claim: The on-disk Ditto store directory is keyed by the user-editable database *name*, but renaming a database in the editor never moves that directory — the rename silently abandons the existing local store, the app opens an empty one in its place, and the original directory is orphaned on disk forever.
actionable.evidence:
`DittoManager.localDirectoryPath(for:)` builds the path from the name (verified at lines 609-618):
```swift
609:        let dbname = databaseConfig.name.trimmingCharacters(
610:            in: .whitespacesAndNewlines
611:        ).lowercased()
...
617:            .appendingPathComponent("\(dbname)-\(databaseConfig.databaseId)")
```
`hydrateDittoSelectedDatabase` appends `database`, creates the path if absent, and hands it to `Ditto.open` (DittoManager.swift:116-127, 172-176 — verified). The name is fully editable for an existing config: `SwiftUI/EdgeStudio/Views/Database/DatabaseEditorView.swift:61` is `TextField("Name", text: $viewModel.name)` with no `.disabled(...)`, in deliberate contrast to the adjacent Database ID field at line 76-83 (`.disabled(!viewModel.isNewItem)`) whose comment at lines 68-75 gives the reason: "It also names the on-disk Ditto store directory (`DittoManager.localDirectoryPath`), so changing it would orphan the local data." `SQLCipherService.updateDatabaseConfig` persists the rename — its `SET` list at line 771 begins `SET name = ?` — and its own doc comment at lines 763-767 states the identical hazard verbatim ("`DittoManager.localDirectoryPath` embeds `name-databaseId`, so changing the column without moving that directory would orphan the local data") while guarding only `databaseId`. `grep -rn "moveItem" SwiftUI/EdgeStudio` returns no hit anywhere in the codebase.
actionable.failure_scenario: A user has a database registered as "Prod" with locally-inserted documents and attachments (or a `.smallPeerOnly` database that has no cloud copy at all). They rename it to "Production" in the editor and press Save. On the next open, `localDirectoryPath` resolves to `…/production-<id>` instead of `…/prod-<id>`, so `Ditto.open` creates a brand-new empty store and every collection appears empty. Deleting the config afterwards runs `FileManager.removeItem` against the *new* empty path (DatabaseRepository.swift:264-267), so the real store at `…/prod-<id>` is left on disk permanently with no way to reach it from the app.

actionable.failure_scenario: A user registers a database in Small Peer Only mode, imports documents into it, then deletes the configuration. `deleteDittoAppConfig` removes `…/ditto_edge_studio/<name>-<id>`, which the SDK never used and which contains nothing but the empty `database/` folder — it logs "Deleted database files at: …" and the user is told the data is gone, while the actual Ditto store (every document, attachment, and the offline license state) remains in the SDK default location indefinitely, invisible to the app. Separately, opening Log Analyzer for that database passes `activePersistenceDirectory` to `LogFileParser.parseDittoLogs(persistenceDirectory:)` (LoggingDetailView.swift:138/870, MCPToolHandlers.swift:879), finds no `ditto_logs/` under the empty directory, and reports zero SDK log entries — a silently broken feature on this mode only.

actionable.claim: `get_app_logs` and `get_ditto_logs` pass an unvalidated caller-supplied `lines` value straight to `Collection.suffix(_:)`, whose precondition traps on negative lengths and kills the whole Edge Studio process.
actionable.evidence: Verified: line 853 `let maxLines = arguments["lines"] as? Int ?? 200` then line 869 `return Array(filtered.suffix(maxLines)).joined(separator: "\n")`; the identical pattern repeats in `getDittoLogs` at line 875 and line 911 `filtered = Array(filtered.suffix(maxLines))`. There is no `max(0, …)` clamp. `arguments` is the raw dictionary from the JSON-RPC body — `MCPJSONRPCHandler.toolsCallResponse` does `let arguments = params["arguments"] as? [String: Any] ?? [:]` (MCPJSONRPCHandler.swift:118) and passes it verbatim to `MCPToolHandlers.execute`; nothing validates arguments against the declared schema anywhere between the socket and these lines. The `inputSchema` for both tools declares only `"type": "integer"` with no `minimum` (lines 235-238 and 252-255), so an LLM client is not steered away from negatives either. JSON `-1` bridges through NSNumber and casts cleanly to `Int(-1)`. Confirmed empirically on this machine (Apple Swift 6.4): `Array(["a","b","c"].suffix(-1))` aborts with `Swift/BidirectionalCollection.swift:411: Fatal error: Can't take a suffix of negative length from a collection`. The trap is uncatchable and the handler runs in-process.
actionable.failure_scenario: With the MCP server enabled, an agent (or any local process) sends `POST /mcp` with `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_app_logs","arguments":{"lines":-1}}}` — a plausible LLM encoding of "give me all the lines". Edge Studio dies instantly with SIGTRAP, taking down the open database session, unsaved query-editor content, and any in-flight sync or import. Same for `get_ditto_logs`.

actionable.claim: The MCP HTTP surface performs no `Origin`/`Host` validation, no Content-Type check and no authentication, so any web page the user visits can silently drive the mutating tools (`execute_dql`, `set_sync`, `drop_index`, `configure_transport`) against the developer's active Ditto database; the mitigation the docs claim does not stop the request from executing.
actionable.evidence: Verified: `handleRequest` routes on method+path only — `case ("POST", "/mcp"): await handlePostMessage(request)` at line 177. `MCPHTTPParser.tryParse` *does* collect every header into `request.headers` (MCPHTTPParser.swift:133-140), but `grep -rniE "origin|authorization|bearer|sec-fetch" SwiftUI/EdgeStudio/Data/MCPServer/` returns zero header reads — the only matches are prose inside tool descriptions. Nothing consults `Origin`, `Host`, `Sec-Fetch-Site`, or any shared secret; the only headers the parser's consumers ever act on are `content-length` and `transfer-encoding`. `handlePostMessage` (lines 227-261) reads only `request.queryParams["sessionId"]` and enforces the session guard *only if one was supplied* — its own comment calls a request with no sessionId "the documented stateless path (direct HTTP transport clients)" and exempts it. `MCPJSONRPCHandler.handle` then does `JSONSerialization.jsonObject(with: body)` (line 49) with no content-type check. docs/MCP_SERVER.md:384 states the defense verbatim: "The server emits no CORS headers and does not answer CORS preflight requests — browser-based clients are not supported; MCP clients are CLI agents, not browsers". That is not a defense: `fetch('http://localhost:65269/mcp',{method:'POST',body:'…'})` sends `Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8`, making it a CORS *simple request* — no preflight is issued, the browser delivers it, and missing CORS response headers only stop the page from *reading* the reply. The side effect has already happened. (Chrome's Private Network Access may prompt; Safari — the macOS default — and Firefox do not implement it.)
actionable.failure_scenario: A developer has Edge Studio open with a production database selected and the MCP server enabled (the documented steady state for agent work) and browses in Safari. Any page they load — an ad frame is enough — POSTs `tools/call` → `execute_dql` with `EVICT FROM orders WHERE true`, then `set_sync {"enabled": false}`. Documents are evicted from the local store and the eviction replicates, replication stops, and the user sees no prompt and no trace except the app log — the UI shows only that the collection is now empty. The same vector reaches `drop_index`, `configure_transport`, and `insert_documents_from_file` with an arbitrary path.

actionable.claim: `applyTransportConfig` early-returns unless `currentStep == .idle`, but `currentStep` is never reset to `.idle` after `.complete` or `.error`, so every subsequent Apply in the same popover session is a silent no-op while the button stays enabled and the green "Configuration applied successfully" banner still shows — the toggles and the banner describe transports that are not actually in effect.
actionable.evidence: Line 347: `guard currentStep == .idle else { return }`, then `currentStep = .stoppingSync`. A full grep of the file for `currentStep` (verified) shows writes only at 306 (initial `.idle`), 348 `.stoppingSync`, 358 `.applyingConfig`, 397 `.restartingSync`, 424 `.complete`, 434 `.error(...)` — no path back to `.idle`, and `loadCurrentSettings()` (the `.task` at line 184) only assigns the `is*`/`original*` pairs. The button gate at line 177 is only `.disabled(viewModel.currentStep.isInProgress || !viewModel.hasChanges || !viewModel.isMulticastInputValid)`; after `.complete`/`.error` `isInProgress` is false, and the success path re-baselines `original*` (lines 426-432) so flipping any toggle makes `hasChanges` (lines 310-319) true again and re-enables the button.
actionable.failure_scenario: macOS: Presence -> gear (Transport Settings). Turn Bluetooth LE off, press Apply — succeeds, banner turns green. Without dismissing the popover also turn LAN off; Apply re-enables. Press it: the guard fails (state is `.complete`), the function returns immediately — no sync stop, no `applyTransportConfig`, no `updateDittoAppConfig`. LAN shows as off and the success banner remains, but LAN is still enabled, still syncing, and nothing was written to disk. Identical dead end after `.error`: every retry press is a no-op, so the popover must be dismissed and reopened to recover, with no indication of that.

actionable.claim: The Add Index sheet iterates its field rows with index-derived bindings (`ForEach(Array($fields.enumerated()))`) while each row owns a button that removes itself from the array — the exact self-removal-through-a-stale-index-binding pattern this repo already documented as crashing and eliminated everywhere else.
actionable.evidence: Line 31: `ForEach(Array($fields.enumerated()), id: \.element.id) { index, $field in`, with `TextField("Field \(index + 1)", text: $field.name)` (33), `DittoSegmentedPicker(options: [true, false], selection: $field.ascending)` (36-38), and inside the same row body `if fields.count > 1 { Button { fields.removeAll { $0.id == field.id } } ... }` (40-42). `$fields.enumerated()` materialises `Binding<FieldDraft>` values that are unchecked `$fields[i]` subscript projections. `DatabaseEditorView.swift:610-614` states the rule verbatim: "Rows are iterated by value and their fields bound through the view model by index, resolved on access. Binding-based `ForEach($rows)` iteration crashes when a row removes itself: the row body owns an index-derived binding that the removal invalidates before `ForEach` re-diffs." AddIndexView:31 is the only remaining binding-based `ForEach` in the view/component tree.
actionable.failure_scenario: Sidebar `+` menu -> Add Index -> tap "Add Field" so `fields.count > 1` (the minus button only renders then, line 40), type into the last row so its TextField is first responder, then tap that row's minus button. `fields.removeAll` drops the last index while the disappearing row's body still reads `$fields[i]` during teardown/resign-first-responder, trapping with "Fatal error: Index out of range" and killing the app with the user's unsaved index definition.

actionable.claim: The iOS/iPadOS `updateUIView` pushes the binding value back into the `UITextView` without the first-responder guard the macOS branch carries specifically to stop in-flight typing from being truncated, so a re-render during typing can revert characters in the Query Workbench editor.
actionable.evidence: iOS, line 219: `func updateUIView(_ uiView: UITextView, context: Context) { context.coordinator.parent = self; if uiView.text != text { let selected = uiView.selectedRange; context.coordinator.isApplyingHighlight = true; uiView.text = text; uiView.selectedRange = selected ... } }` — no first-responder test. macOS `updateNSView` (lines 84-99) guards exactly this: `let isEditing = textView.window?.firstResponder === textView` / `if textView.string != text, !isEditing {`, with the comment "While the text view is being edited it is the source of truth — resetting it here to a binding value that lags behind by a render cycle truncates in-flight input (fast/programmatic typing loses everything after the lag point)." `text` is the value snapshotted when SwiftUI last evaluated `body`, and the editor's host re-renders frequently (`DetailViews.swift` reads live sync/presence state in the same body).
actionable.failure_scenario: On iPad, type or paste quickly (or dictate) into the query editor while peers are connected and the presence observer is ticking. `textViewDidChange` writes the binding; further keystrokes land in the text view before `updateUIView` runs; when it does, `uiView.text` ("SELECT * FROM orders") != the stale `text` ("SELECT * FROM ord"), so the text view is reset to the shorter string, silently dropping everything typed since that render, clearing highlighting and leaving the caret at a now-invalid offset. The same overwrite drops in-flight IME/dictation composition. macOS is unaffected because of the `isEditing` guard.

actionable.claim: The Presence Viewer's zoom percentage readout prints the raw SpriteKit camera scale as if it were magnification, which is its inverse — pressing "+" (zoom in) makes the displayed percentage go down, and fully zoomed out reads "400%".
actionable.evidence: Verified at PresenceViewerSK.swift:853-856: `Text("\(Int(viewModel.zoomLevel * 100))%")` with `.accessibilityLabel("Zoom level \(Int(viewModel.zoomLevel * 100)) percent")`. `zoomLevel` *is* the camera scale: `func updateZoomLevel(_ level: CGFloat) { zoomLevel = level; scene?.camera?.setScale(level) }` (line 724-726). A larger SKCameraNode scale shows MORE of the scene; the code says so itself — `zoomIn()` DECREASES the value (`let newZoom = max(0.5, zoomLevel - 0.1)`, line 710) and `zoomOut()` increases it toward 4.0 (line 718, commented "4.0 camera scale = the VS Code extension's 0.25 minimum magnification"), and `PresenceFocusPlanner.focusCameraScale` states "scale = 1/magnification, so 1.25× magnification is scale 0.8". `docs/PRESENCE_GRAPH.md` specifies the user-facing range as 0.25×–2.0× magnification (camera scale 0.5–4.0), i.e. the readout should be 25%–200%, not 50%–400% reversed. The button disabled states (`.disabled(viewModel.zoomLevel >= 4.0)` on zoom-out at line 848, `<= 0.5` on zoom-in at line 866) then contradict the label.

Clicking "−" to the limit shows "400%" while the graph is at 0.25× magnification, and the zoom-out button disables at the number's maximum. Entering focus mode fires `onZoomChanged?(0.8)` for a view documented as magnifying to at least 1.25×, so it reports "80%" to the screen and to VoiceOver.

actionable.claim: Saving a database config whose `databaseId` already exists silently REPLACEs the existing row and, because foreign keys are ON, cascade-deletes every subscription, observer, favorite and history row belonging to that database — with no warning and no undo.
actionable.evidence:
Verified in source. `DatabaseRepositoryImpl.save` routes every `id == 0L` config to the REPLACE insert:
```kotlin
override suspend fun save(database: DittoDatabase): Long = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    if (database.id == 0L) {
        ...
        dao.insert(database.toEntity())
```
`DatabaseConfigDao.kt:26` declares `@Insert(onConflict = OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE)  suspend fun insert(entity: DatabaseConfigEntity): Long`. `DatabaseConfigEntity.kt:10` makes the conflict reachable: `indices = [Index(value = ["databaseId"], unique = true)]`. `SubscriptionEntity.kt:16`, `ObservableEntity.kt:16`, `HistoryEntity.kt:16` and `FavoriteEntity.kt:16` each declare `ForeignKey(entity = DatabaseConfigEntity::class, parentColumns = ["databaseId"], childColumns = ["databaseId"], onDelete = ForeignKey.CASCADE)`, and the generated `AppDatabase_Impl.kt:99` runs `connection.execSQL("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")`, so the cascade is live. Both reviewers independently reproduced the semantics in sqlite3 against the same schema shape: after an `INSERT OR REPLACE` on the conflicting unique key the child rows went to 0 and the parent row got a new rowid. Nothing on the way in checks for an existing `databaseId`: `QrScannerViewModel.kt:60` calls `databaseRepository.save(result.database)` on a `DittoDatabase` that `QrCodeDecoder.toDittoDatabase()` (QrCodeDecoder.kt:135) builds with the default `id = 0`, and `DatabaseEditorViewModel.canSave` (line 115) gates only on non-blank name/databaseId/token.
actionable.failure_scenario: A user has database "Prod" (databaseId `abc`) with saved subscriptions, observers, favorites and query history. A teammate shares the same database as a QR code (or the user re-scans their own share QR, or hand-types a config with the same App ID in the New Database editor). `QrScannerViewModel.processBarcode` → `save` → `dao.insert` → REPLACE fires on the unique `databaseId` index: the old config row is deleted, the CASCADE wipes every subscription, observer, favorite and history row for `abc`, and a fresh config row with a new `_id` is inserted. The UI reports `QrScannerUiState.Success` — no warning, no confirmation, no undo.

actionable.claim: `activeHandles` and `activeObserverHandles` are plain unsynchronized `LinkedHashMap`s mutated from both the main thread (Compose click handlers, Koin `onClose`) and `Dispatchers.IO` session coroutines; `close()` iterates them on the main thread while those coroutines are still live, which can throw `ConcurrentModificationException` out of Compose disposal or silently drop an SDK handle that is then never closed.
actionable.evidence: Verified in source. Declarations carry no synchronization: line 138 `private val activeHandles = mutableMapOf<Long, DittoSyncSubscription>()` and line 144 `private val activeObserverHandles = mutableMapOf<Long, DittoStoreObserver>()`. Main-thread writers: `activateObserver` is a plain non-suspend function doing `activeObserverHandles[observer.id] = handle` (line 683) and `deactivateObserver` does `activeObserverHandles.remove(observer.id)?.close()` (line 694), both reached synchronously from Compose — `ObserversListPane.kt:129 viewModel.activateObserver(observer)` / `:133 onDeactivate = { viewModel.deactivateObserver(observer) }` → `MainStudioViewModel.kt:295 fun activateObserver(observer) = session.activateObserver(observer)`, no coroutine hop. Background writers on `sessionScope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + ioDispatcher)` (line 85, `ioDispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO`, line 77): `updateObserver` line 625, `removeObserver` line 646, `addSubscriptionSuspend` line 550, `updateSubscription` lines 572/575, `removeSubscription` line 590. `close()` then iterates on the main thread (`StudioScopeManager.kt:47 onDispose { scope.close() }` → Koin `onClose { it?.close() }`): line 826 `activeHandles.values.forEach { runCatching { it.close() } }` and line 829 `activeObserverHandles.values.forEach { runCatching { it.close() } }`. The `runCatching` sits inside the loop body, so a `ConcurrentModificationException` raised by the iterator itself is not caught, and `sessionScope.cancel()` is only reached later in `close()`, so those coroutines are still running during the iteration. The file's own KDoc documents exactly this hazard for the observer *event* pipeline and guards it with `synchronized(observerEventPipelineLock)` (used at line 834) — the handle maps got no such guard.
actionable.failure_scenario: The user taps Delete on a subscription (or observer) and immediately presses Back to leave the studio. `removeSubscription`'s coroutine runs `activeHandles.remove(id)` on a Dispatchers.IO thread while `close()` on the main thread is part-way through `activeHandles.values.forEach { ... }`; the iterator sees the changed modCount and throws `ConcurrentModificationException` out of `DisposableEffect.onDispose`, crashing the app on exit. The milder variant: activating observer A on the main thread while a delete of observer B mutates the map on IO loses A's put, so A's `DittoStoreObserver` handle is never recorded, `close()` never closes it, and the SDK observer keeps firing callbacks for the rest of the process lifetime.

actionable.claim: `applyTransportSettings` unconditionally restarts sync in its `finally` block even when the user had deliberately stopped sync, and never updates `_syncEnabled` — so replication resumes while the toolbar still shows sync as off.
actionable.evidence: Verified in source. `applyTransportSettings` stops sync (`ditto.sync.stop()`) and then, in a `finally` that runs on every path, line 780: `runCatching { dittoManager.startSync() }` followed by `runCatching { systemRepository.startObserving(ditto) }`. `DittoManager.startSync()` is not conditional — it re-runs the full open sequence whose last step is `instance.sync.start()`. Nothing in `applyTransportSettings` touches `_syncEnabled`; grep over the file shows it is written in exactly three places: line 478 (`hydrate` → true), line 518 (`toggleSync` stop → false) and line 525 (`toggleSync` start → true). The toolbar reads exactly that flag: `StudioScaffold.kt:137 val syncEnabled by session.syncEnabled.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()`, driving the indicator tint at `:208` (`if (syncEnabled) Color(0xFF34C759) else ...`) and `:328`. The sheet is reachable with sync off — `PresenceSection.kt:359` shows the `ModalBottomSheet { TransportConfigContent(viewModel) }` with no sync-state gate, and its Apply button (`TransportConfigSheet.kt:206`) is enabled whenever `!isApplyingTransport && multicastValid`.
actionable.failure_scenario: A user debugging mesh behaviour taps the sync toggle to stop replication (`_syncEnabled = false`, indicator grey). Still in the Presence section they open the transport gear sheet, turn Bluetooth off and tap Apply. The `finally` calls `dittoManager.startSync()` — the device is syncing and replicating again — while the toolbar indicator stays grey, reporting sync as off. The user believes the device is isolated and draws wrong conclusions from everything observed afterwards. The state only self-corrects if they tap the toggle again, which reads `ditto.sync.isActive == true` and stops it, so that first tap appears to do nothing.

actionable.claim: On tablet/expanded widths the database editor's ViewModel key is derived from a plain `remember` counter that resets whenever DatabaseListScreen leaves the composition, while the NavEntry ViewModelStore survives — so a later edit re-uses a retained ViewModel constructed for a DIFFERENT database row. The editor displays and then overwrites the wrong database.
actionable.evidence: Verified at DatabaseListScreen.kt:86-94: `var tabletEditorId by remember { mutableStateOf<Long?>(null) }`, `var tabletEditorSession by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }` (plain `remember`, not `rememberSaveable`), `onAddDatabase = { tabletEditorId = -1L; tabletEditorSession++ }`, `onEditDatabase = { db -> tabletEditorId = db.id; tabletEditorSession++ }`. Verified at DatabaseListScreen.kt:113-117: `DatabaseEditorScreen(databaseId = id, instanceKey = "tablet_editor_$tabletEditorSession", onDismiss = …)`. Verified at DatabaseEditorScreen.kt:70-73: `viewModel: DatabaseEditorViewModel = koinViewModel(key = instanceKey, parameters = { parametersOf(databaseId) })`. ViewModelProvider returns an existing instance for a key without invoking the Koin factory, so `parametersOf(databaseId)` is ignored on a key collision. editId is baked in at construction — DataModule.kt:233 `viewModel { (editId: Long) -> DatabaseEditorViewModel(editId, get(), get()) }` — and DatabaseEditorViewModel.kt:22/27/381 confirm `private val editId: Long`, `val isNewItem: Boolean get() = editId <= 0L`, and `id = if (isNewItem) 0L else editId` in the save path. The VMs live in the DatabaseListKey nav entry's ViewModelStore (AppNavGraph.kt entryDecorators list contains exactly `rememberSaveableStateHolderNavEntryDecorator()` and `rememberViewModelStoreNavEntryDecorator()`), and DatabaseListKey is the never-popped root key. Nothing ever clears accumulated `tablet_editor_N` ViewModels.
actionable.failure_scenario: Tablet (≥600dp). 1) Long-press database A → Edit: `tabletEditorSession` becomes 1, VM "tablet_editor_1" is created with editId = A. 2) Dismiss. 3) Tap any card to open the studio — DatabaseListScreen leaves the composition and `tabletEditorSession` (plain `remember`) is discarded; the entry's ViewModelStore is retained. 4) Close the studio back to the list; `tabletEditorSession` is 0 again. 5) Long-press database B → Edit: session becomes 1, so `koinViewModel(key = "tablet_editor_1")` returns the retained VM for A. The dialog shows A's name, databaseId, token and HTTP API key under an "Edit Database" title. The user edits what they believe is B and taps Save — `dao.update()` runs against row A. B is untouched; A's production config is destroyed. A screen rotation reproduces the same collision.

actionable.claim: The Log Analyzer's Export action writes the entire in-memory log buffer (up to 20,000 entries on the Ditto SDK tab) to the SAF-chosen output stream synchronously on the main/UI dispatcher, freezing the app for the duration of the write and risking an ANR.
actionable.evidence: `scope` is the composition scope, i.e. AndroidUiDispatcher.Main (LoggingScreen.kt:120 `val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()`). The SAF `CreateDocument` result callback launches into it with no dispatcher switch (lines 195-197): `scope.launch { exportError = exportLogEntries(context, uri, entries) }`. `exportLogEntries` is a plain, non-suspend blocking function with no `withContext` (LoggingScreen.kt:1049-1066): `context.contentResolver.openOutputStream(uri)?.bufferedWriter()?.use { writer -> entries.forEach { entry -> writer.append(iso.format(entry.timestamp))… ; writer.newLine() } }` — one `SimpleDateFormat.format` plus several appends per entry. The payload is deliberately the whole retained buffer, not the rendered rows: the comment at lines 183-184 reads "Exports the full in-memory buffer, not just the visible 200 rows", and `entries` is the raw tab buffer (lines 189-194 `0 -> sdkEntries` …). `DittoLogCaptureService` retains `MAX_HISTORICAL_ENTRIES = 10_000` plus `MAX_LIVE_ENTRIES = 10_000` (DittoLogCaptureService.kt:50-51) and `sdkEntries` is the merge of both, so up to 20,000 records. Every other I/O path in this file and package correctly offloads — `loadHistoricalLogs` / `loadAppLogs` in the same screen, QueryWorkbenchSection.kt:274 `exportScope.launch(kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers.IO)`, ImportJsonSheet.kt:78 `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` — so the omission here is a defect, not house style.
actionable.failure_scenario: Run a Debug/Verbose capture on the Ditto SDK tab until the buffer fills (the screen's own 'High log volume' banner appears), tap Export in the footer and pick a destination served by a network-backed document provider (Drive, OneDrive, SMB). The result callback runs on the main thread: `openOutputStream` performs a binder round-trip and ~20,000 blocking append/newLine calls stream through it, all on the UI thread. The screen stops drawing and stops responding to scrolling, the pause button and Back; on a slow provider this exceeds the 5 s input-dispatch window and Android shows the 'isn't responding' dialog. - The window is narrow. The re-appearance has to be applied by a flush that lands before the fade completes, i.e. the peer must return roughly 0–300 ms after its removal was rendered.

The only precondition is `guard data.count > 18`, which a truncated multi-KB archive passes trivially. That uncertainty affects frequency, not validity: the guard is absent, the path is default-on, and a single malformed file in `ditto_logs/` (rotation interrupted by a force-quit, an incomplete transfer, or any mis-named file in an imported folder) is sufficient. adjudication.reasoning:
I looked for a guard and could not find one; every link in the chain checks out against the code and against the exact Compose artifacts this build resolves.

The claim's core assertion — that `Modifier.pointerInput(ref.id)` keeps running the lambda instance captured at the row's first touch — is not speculative here. `SuspendPointerInputElement.equals` does compare the handler by `Intrinsics.areEqual`, so a new capturing lambda each recomposition makes the element unequal and `update$ui` runs; but `update$ui` only resets when a key differs or the handler's *class* differs, and a Kotlin lambda from one call site is the same class on every recomposition. The field is swapped while the already-launched, never-completing `awaitEachGesture` coroutine keeps invoking the original instance. That is the well-known "stale capture in pointerInput" hazard, and the standard remedy (`rememberUpdatedState`, or keying on the mutable value) is absent from this call site.

The two things that could have refuted it both fail to:
- Row teardown between drags would restart the coroutine and hide the bug. It does not happen: `key(ref.id)` makes Compose *move* the keyed group, `LayoutNode.move$ui` re-slots without detaching, and `userScrollEnabled = !isReordering` keeps the LazyColumn item composed for the whole mode. The file's own comment at 585-592 states this identity preservation as the intended design, so it is not incidental.
- Live state reads would mask it. Only partly: `dragStartIndex`, `dropIndex` and `dragOffset` are `MutableState` delegates read live, but `index` (written into `dragStartIndex` at line 652) and `displayed` (lines 661 and 668) are plain captured values, and `displayed` provably changes after a drop because `onDragEnd` itself assigns `workingPins = reordered` at line 672.

Reachability is ordinary, not theoretical: reorder mode is explicitly a mode you stay in (the toggle at line 567 reads "Done"), so making two moves without leaving it is the expected interaction, and the second move of an already-dragged row is the first thing that breaks. The consequence is not cosmetic — `SystemMetricsPinOrdering.move` is applied to the pre-first-drag list and the result is persisted via `onReorder`, so a correct earlier reorder is silently thrown away.

This is a defect, not pre-existing intended behaviour. The design intent recorded in `docs/PINNED_REORDER.md` (Rule 2: never reorder while the drag is in flight, and keep the row's live gesture alive across the reorder) is exactly what preserves the stale node — the intent is sound, the implementation forgot that the surviving gesture also survives with its old captures. The absence of any drag-path test (the androidTest suite drives only the Move Up/Move Down accessibility actions, which go through the correctly-updated `semantics` node) explains why this got past the existing guards.

One honest limit on my confidence: I verified this analytically from source plus bytecode rather than by reproducing it on a device or emulator, which I could not run here. Everything in the chain is directly evidenced, but a manual pass — pin four metrics, enter Reorder, drag the bottom row to the top, then drag that same row again without leaving the mode — would settle it in seconds and is worth doing before and after any fix, per the doc's own manual-pass requirement.

unconfirmed_not_adjudicated.evidence: The expanded content is an unbounded plain Column (LogProblemsSection.kt:105-107): `AnimatedVisibility(visible = expanded) { Column(modifier = Modifier.padding(horizontal = 16.dp, vertical = 4.dp)) { groups.forEach { (key, matches) -> …`, with per-group hit rows at line 146 `matches.take(MAX_SHOWN_HITS_PER_PATTERN).forEach { match ->` (up to 10 rows per expanded group; `MAX_SHOWN_HITS_PER_PATTERN = 10`, line 41). There is no `heightIn`, no `verticalScroll`, and the number of groups is bounded only by the pattern catalog. The parent does not scroll either: LoggingScreen.kt:480 `Column(modifier = modifier.fillMaxSize())`, with the strip composed at LoggingScreen.kt:814, the log list declared after it as a weighted child at LoggingScreen.kt:903 `Box(modifier = Modifier.weight(1f))`, and the footer after that (LoggingScreen.kt:957+). Compose's Column measures unweighted children in declaration order against the remaining main-axis space and only then distributes what is left to weighted children, so a tall unweighted strip starves everything declared after it. The sibling section in the same screen guards exactly this hazard and documents why: LogAnalyticsSection.kt:443-448 `AnimatedVisibility(visible = expanded) { Column(modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth().heightIn(max = HISTOGRAMS_MAX_HEIGHT).verticalScroll(rememberScrollState())…`, with the rationale at lines 95-104 — "The section sits in a [Column] above a weighted log list, so anything it contributes to the minimum height is taken from the list. Bounding it here — and scrolling internally past the bound — is what stops a tall chart from squeezing the log rows off the screen." LogProblemsSection has the same shape and none of that bounding.
unconfirmed_not_adjudicated.failure_scenario: On a phone, a capture matches three bundled patterns (e.g. connection_incomplete, replication_consecutive_resets, deadlock_warning). The user taps the "N problems matched on M log lines" header to expand the strip, then expands two or three groups to read the offending lines — each group is a ~40 dp header plus up to ten ~16 dp hit rows, so roughly 200 dp per expanded group. Past about 400-500 dp the remaining height is exhausted: the weighted log-list Box measures at 0 dp, and the date-range row and Export/Clear footer declared after it measure at 0 dp as well. The screen shows only the problems strip — no log rows, no way to export or clear — until the user works out that collapsing the strip header at the top restores them.
